ABSTRACT: Background: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disease with two pathological features in the brain: amyloid β (Aβ) plaques and tau tangles. Neuroinflammation plays an important role in the development of AD, closely related to both Aβ and tau pathologies. Tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα) and nuclear factor-κB (NFκB) behave as key regulators of neuroinflammation in AD. It is pressing to develop effective AD drugs. Objective: This study aimed to explore the effects and mechanisms of quercetagitrin in AD using a combination of network pharmacology analyses and in vivo experiments. Methods: The potential target of quercetagitrin in AD was predicted by network pharmacology. The interaction between the compound and the target protein was measured by molecular docking. The in vivo effects were performed in APP/PS1 mice via mouse behavior tests, Western blotting, ThS staining, immunohistochemical staining, and immunofluorescence staining. Results: First, network pharmacology analyses were conducted to predict the primary target of the compound, which is TNFα. Then, molecular docking showed that quercetagitrin interacts with TNFα with a high affinity. Finally, the level of TNFα was reduced, and the activation of NFκB signaling was inhibited by quercetagitrin in APP/PS1 mice. Meanwhile, quercetagitrin treatment ameliorated Aβ pathology, cognitive impairments, and neuroinflammation in the AD mice. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate quercetagitrin as a potential therapeutic drug for AD.  
1. INTRODUCTION: exacerbating neuronal damage. Neuroinflammation has been considered another critical hallmark of AD.7 Gene-regulatory network analysis of postmortem brain tissues from AD patients showed that neuroinflammation not only participates in the progression of AD but also is involved in the onset.8 Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) plays a critical role in mammalian inflammatory responses. It leads to inflammation either by stimulating inflammatory gene expression or triggering cell death.9 Binding of TNF to TNF receptor 1 (TNFR1) promotes inflammation via the activation of the nuclear factor-κB (NFκB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathways, collectively resulting in the transcriptional increase of genes encoding proinflammatory factors.10 TNFα, the commonest form of TNF, was shown to upregulate the activity of BACE1, as well as NFκB, which are directly responsible for the production of Aβ.11 Quercetagitrin (6-hydroxyquercetin 7-O-β-glucopyranoside) is a natural flavonoid compound extracted mainly from marigold (Tagetes erecta L.), originally from Mexico and now worldwide. Traditionally, T. erecta is utilized as a medicinal plant, tea, cooking ingredient, and food colorant. Quercetagitrin has been shown to exhibit antioxidant activities by either metal chelating or lipoxygenase inhibition.12 It also could suppress the catalytic activity of PTPN6 and PTPN9, indicating its potential in type II diabetes treatment.13 In addition, anti-inflammatory effects of quercetagitrin have been reported. For example, it displayed 60% inhibition of lysosomal enzyme secretion and arachidonic acid release in rat neutrophils.14 Our laboratory previously presented that it could attenuate NFκB activation and rescue cognitive deficits by inhibiting tau aggregation in the P301S-tau transgenic mouse model.15 In this study, we applied quercetagitrin to the APP/PS1 mouse model, which is a very popular model for AD studies. First, network pharmacology was performed to explore the target of quercetagitrin in AD, and TNF was predicted. Next, computer-based molecular docking was employed to observe the interaction of the compound and TNFα. Then, the APP/PS1 mice were administered by quercetagitrin. The in vivo experiments illustrated that the compound could improve cognitive disorders and Aβ pathologies and alleviate inflammation via the TNFα/NFκB signaling pathway. Our results provide both computational and experimental evidence for further development of quercetagitrin as a potential drug candidate for AD treatment.  
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS  
2.1. Network Pharmacology Analysis. A comprehensive search was conducted using the keywords “Alzheimer disease” across several databases, including Gene Cards (https://www.genecards.org/), the Therapeutic Target Database (https://db.idrblab.net/ttd/), and the DisGeNET database. The potential therapeutic targets identified from the network pharmacology analysis were uploaded to the STRING database (https://string-db.org/, version 11.0) for further analysis. The species was specified as Homo sapiens, and the network type was set to “full STRING network.” The confidence level was adjusted to “medium confidence (0.400),” and the false discovery rate strictness was set to “medium (5%),” while all other parameters were maintained at their default settings to initially obtain the PPI network data. The resulting PPI network was constructed by Cytoscape (version 3.10.2). Topological analysis was conducted using the “Analyze Network” function within Cytoscape. Core targets were identified through screening based on degree, betweenness centrality, and closeness centrality metrics. The degree values were used to visually highlight the targets.  
2.2. Construction of the PPI Network. The potential therapeutic targets identified from the network pharmacology analysis were uploaded to the Metascape platform (http://metascape.org) for enrichment analysis. The species was designated as H. sapiens, and personalized analysis parameters were configured with a minimum overlap of 3, a P value cutoff of 0.01, and a minimum enrichment threshold of 1.5. The GO enrichment analysis and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis were performed separately.  
2.3. Molecular Docking. The gene names were retrieved from the UniProt database (https://www.uniprot.org/) to obtain the corresponding human protein UniProt IDs. These IDs were then utilized to source the crystal structures from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (https://www.rcsb.org/), specifying H. sapiens as the source organism. Preference was given to crystal structures with low-resolution (Å) values and minimal missing amino acid residues in the active regions relevant to ligand binding. The PDB files of these selected protein structures were downloaded and saved. Additionally, the chemical structure of quercetagitrin was obtained from the TCMSP database and converted to the MOL2 format. Subsequently, the protein structures underwent preprocessing by Chimera software, which involved the removal of water molecules and ligands and the addition of hydrogen atoms. Figure 2A displays the Morris water maze tests to assess anxiety, learning, and memory. In the open-field test, APP/PS1 mice exhibited pronounced anxiety-like behavior compared to C57 mice, with a significantly reduced residence time and movement distance in the central open area. Quercetagitrin treatment markedly improved these anxiety-like behaviors, increasing both residence time and movement distance in the central open area (Figure 3A,B). These differences were not due to variations in movement, as the average move speed showed no significant change among the three groups (Figure 3C). The results suggest that quercetagitrin can ameliorate anxiety-like behavior in 9 month-old APP/PS1 mice. In the novel object recognition experiment, the APP/PS1 mice could not distinguish the old and new objects and even spent more time exploring the old objects. In contrast, both C57 mice and the treated APP/PS1 mice exhibited a significantly higher recognition index in the new objects, suggesting that quercetagitrin treatment enhanced exploratory behavior and cognitive function in APP/PS1 mice (Figure 3D,E). Similarly, the novel position recognition experiment gave the corresponding observation and conclusion (Figure 3F,G). In the Y-maze test, APP/PS1 mice exhibited a significantly lower spontaneous alternation rate compared with C57 mice, while the administration group showed a marked improvement (Figure 3H). The total number of arm entries among the three groups was not significant (Figure 3I). Finally, the Morris water maze test was employed to assess the learning and memory abilities of the mice. During the 5-day training, C57 mice and the treated APP/PS1 mice exhibited superior learning abilities compared with control APP/PS1 mice (Figure 3J). After a 24 h retention period, C57 and the administration mice showed more crossing and residence time in the target platform location compared to control APP/PS1 mice (Figure 3K,L). The results all express that treatment of quercetagitrin improved anxiety-like behaviors and cognitive impairment in APP/PS1 mice. 3.4. Quercetagitrin Protects Neuronal Loss in APP/PS1 Mice. Neuronal loss is a critical pathological feature in AD and serves as the cellular basis for cognitive deficits. In this study, the number of neurons was measured via immunofluorescence staining by the neuronal marker NeuN. As shown in Figure 4, compared to C57 mice, APP/PS1 mice exhibited a significant reduction of neuron numbers in all of the CA1, CA3, and DG regions of the hippocampus and in the cortex. Furthermore, the levels of two synaptic proteins, synaptophysin (SYP) and postsynaptic density protein-95 (PSD-95), were measured in both cortical and hippocampal samples. Synaptophysin is a presynaptic vesicle membrane protein involved in the localized retrieval and recycling of synaptic vesicles after exocytosis. PSD-95 is predominantly exclusively associated with postsynaptic densities. Both proteins are critical for the maintenance of neurotransmission. The levels of the two proteins in both the cortex and hippocampus decreased in the APP/PS1 mice compared to the WT mice but were restored by the treatment of quercetagitrin (Figure 4D,E). So, quercetagitrin could rescue the synaptic functions of the neurons in the brain of the APP/PS1 mice.  
The immunofluorescence and Western blotting results are consistent with those revealed by the behavioral tests. 3.5. Quercetagitrin Alleviates Aβ-Related Pathology in APP/PS1 Mice. To determine whether quercetagitrin treatment can reduce Aβ pathology in APP/PS1 mice, key indicators were assessed using thioflavin S (ThS) staining, immunohistochemistry, and Western blotting. ThS is usually utilized to detect amyloid plaques that possess abundant β-strand structures. ThS staining experiments indicated a significant reduction in fluorescent plaques in both the cortex and hippocampus of quercetagitrin-treated mice compared to control APP/PS1 mice (Figure 5A,B). Then, immunohistochemical staining using the Aβ antibody was performed to further observe the Aβ aggregates. The results also revealed decreased levels of Aβ plaques in the brain of APP/PS1 mice with quercetagitrin, particularly in the cortex (Figure 5C,D). BACE1 and sAPPβ only appear in the amyloidogenic pathway, while sAPPα appears in the nonamyloidogenic pathway.  
Quercetagitrin inhibited Aβ aggregation in a dose-dependent manner, as shown by the reduced Aβ fibrillization (Figure S3). The results indicate that quercetagitrin could directly inhibit Aβ aggregation in vitro. 3.6. Quercetagitrin Reduces Neuroinflammation in APP/PS1 Mice. Based on the results of network pharmacology, TNF is one of the most likely therapeutic targets (Figure 1C). TNF is a proinflammatory cytokine that participates in the neuroinflammatory response in vivo. So, we explored whether quercetagitrin could mitigate neuroinflammation via the TNFα/signaling pathway in APP/PS1 mice. Astrocytes and microglia are the two primary immune cells in the brain. Immunofluorescence staining revealed significantly elevated levels of astrocyte marker GFAP and microglial marker Iba1 in the hippocampus of APP/PS1 mice compared with C57 mice. Notably, the fluorescence intensity of the two markers was markedly reduced upon the treatment of quercetagitrin (Figure 6A,B). Subsequently, Western blot analysis demonstrated a significant reduction in TNFα protein levels in both the hippocampus and cortex of APP/PS1 mice treated with quercetagitrin (Figure 6C,D). TNF can indirectly activate NFκB, leading to the formation of phosphorylated NFκB (p-NFκB). Finally, Western blotting was performed to detect the levels of total NFκB, p-NFκB, and two downstream inflammatory factors: nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). Expectedly, a decrease in both p-NFκB (S468)/total NFκB and p-NFκB (S536)/total NFκB was observed in the treatment group. The levels of iNOS and COX-2 were reduced as well upon quercetagitrin (Figure 6E,F). Collectively, these results suggest that quercetagitrin effectively mitigates neuroinflammation through the TNFα/NFκB pathway in APP/PS1 mice.  
4. DISCUSSION  
Network pharmacology was first proposed in year 2007, and it is an approach combining chemogenomics with network biology for drug discovery. It highlights the comprehensive effects of disease or syndrome biological networks as targets to clarify the general regulatory mechanism of herbal constituents. Recently, this technology has been used a lot to elucidate the application of traditional medicine in various kinds of diseases, including AD. For example, polymethoxy-lated flavones, the key lipid-soluble components in Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium, have been predicted and validated to inhibit neuroinflammation in AD mouse models. Berberine ameliorates AD pathological features by inhibiting the JNK-P38MAPK pathway and ferroptosis, further reducing Aβ plaque deposition and inhibiting inflammatory response in 5× FAD mice. Aucubin alleviates cognitive and memory deficits, AD-like pathologies of the mouse brain, including the deposition of Aβ plaques and neuronal damage, and keratinocytes. .34 inflammatory responses by inhibiting the ERK/FOS axis in Quercetagitrin is a polyphenol flavonoid molecule extracted from APP/PS1 mice.21 The combination of network pharmacology mainly from Tagetes erecta L. The polyphenol-enriched extracts and experiments revealed that steamed Panax notoginseng from T. erecta L. inhibited glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) activity and promoted β-catenin nuclear translocation in Aβ content in the brain of AD Drosophila models and MC3T3-E1 cells.35 Actually, GSK-3β also behaves as the primary kinase on tau hyperphosphorylation in AD. Besides Aβ plaques, neurofibrillary tangles consisting of hyperphosphorylated tau are another clinical pathology in the brain of AD patients. Our previous article showed that quercetagitrin alone could reduce tau phosphorylation at different residues via GSK-3β inhibition in PS19 mice and tau-overexpressed HEK293 and N2a cells.15 One fraction (containing over 85% quercetagitrin) from T. erecta L. displayed antioxidant activities, which are metal-chelating activity and lipoxygenase inhibition.12 The balance of metal ions is essential for human health, especially in the central nervous system, while metal ions participate in the development of AD.36 The levels of Zn2+, Cu2+ ions, and Fe2+ ions are all elevated in the AD brain. So, the metal-chelating activity of quercetagitrin could be beneficial to AD treatment from another perspective. 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX) is a proinflammatory enzyme that mediates inflammation, and abnormal activation of 5-LOX has been shown in the development of age-related brain pathology, suggesting the inhibition of 5-LOX activation as a promising therapeutic direction for AD.37 The lipoxygenase inhibition function of quercetagitrin plays a positive role in AD treatment. In addition, our current results showed that quercetagitrin reduced Aβ plaques in the mice, possibly due to the direct inhibition of Aβ aggregation as it did in vitro. However, more experiments should be carried out to elaborate on this point. AD is a complicated neurodegenerative disease with various inducers, and the current drug acting on a one-single target cannot prevent or cure the disease very well. Thus, the utilization of multiple interventions against several molecular targets of AD pathologies might be the most practical approach to curing the disease.38 Considering the various bioactive functions summarized above, quercetagitrin might be a potential leading compound for the treatment of AD. In conclusion, quercetagitrin could improve the recognitive deficits, reduce Aβ levels, and ameliorate neuroinflammation, likely implicating the TNFα/NFκB pathway in APP/PS1 mice. ■ ASSOCIATED CONTENT Data Availability Statement The data are available throughout the manuscript and supporting files. * Supporting Information The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsomega.5c05682.
